subject: All Subjects
summary: the most-repeated GATE traps across the syllabus: successive percentages, counting with a leading zero, limits in degrees, a non-linear ODE that blows up, trace of A², kinetic energy of a rolling ring, volumetric strain under uniaxial load, the hollow-shaft k⁴ rule, the redundant roller in a cam, static deflection and frequency, Darcy versus Fanning friction factor, local versus average h, Carnot COP in kelvin, I²R heating and the EOQ holding cost — each solution names the trap so you can avoid it on exam day

questions.text: The price of an article is first raised by 10 % and later the new price is reduced by 10 %. Compared with the original price, the final price is
solution: Concept: Successive percentage changes multiply; they do not add. Net factor = (1 + a)(1 + b).
The final price is 1 % lower (A) than the original.
Exam tip: Two equal and opposite percentage changes always give a net loss of (x/10)² %: here (10/10)² = 1 %. The order of the two changes does not matter.

questions.text: The number of three-digit positive integers (100 to 999) in which all three digits are different is ______
solution: Concept: Fill the places one at a time, starting with the most restricted place (fundamental counting principle).
Hundreds digit: 9 choices (1–9, zero not allowed). Tens digit: 9 choices (0–9 except the hundreds digit). Units digit: 8 choices.
Exam tip: Starting with 10 × 9 × 8 = 720 forgets that a number cannot begin with 0; 720 − 72 (those starting with 0) = 648 is the same answer by subtraction.

questions.text: If x is measured in degrees, the value of the limit of (sin x)/x as x → 0 is
solution: Concept: The standard result sin θ/θ → 1 holds only when θ is in radians.
x degrees = πx/180 radians, so sin x° = sin(πx/180).
Exam tip: The same trap appears in calculus with angles: d/dx (sin x°) = (π/180) cos x°. Always convert to radians before differentiating, integrating or taking limits.

questions.text: The solution of dy/dx = y² with y(0) = 1/2 is y = 1/(2 − x). Which one of the following statements is correct?
opts: The solution is valid for all real x, and y(3) = −1
The solution exists only for x < 2; it becomes unbounded as x → 2
The solution exists only for x > 2
The equation has no solution through (0, 1/2) because it is non-linear
questions.ans: (B) The solution exists only for x < 2; it becomes unbounded as x → 2
solution: Concept: For a non-linear equation the solution through a given point may exist only on a limited interval, which must contain the starting point and on which y stays finite.
Separating variables: −1/y = x + c; y(0) = 1/2 gives c = −2, so y = 1/(2 − x).
y → ∞ as x → 2⁻, so the solution through (0, 1/2) lives only on −∞ < x < 2: option (B). Substituting x = 3 into the formula (y = −1) gives a point on a different branch, not on this solution.
Exam tip: dy/dx = y² is always ≥ 0, so a solution cannot drop from +∞ to −1; checking the sign of the slope catches the trap at once.

questions.text: A 3 × 3 matrix A has the eigenvalues 1, 2 and −3. The trace of A² is ______
solution: Concept: If λ is an eigenvalue of A, then λ² is an eigenvalue of A². The trace of any matrix equals the sum of its eigenvalues.
Eigenvalues of A²: 1, 4 and 9.
Exam tip: Squaring the trace, (1 + 2 − 3)² = 0, is the trap: trace(A²) = Σλ², not (Σλ)².

questions.text: A thin ring (hoop) of mass 2 kg rolls without slipping on a level floor; the speed of its centre is 3 m/s. Its total kinetic energy (in J) is ______
solution: Concept: For rolling without slipping, KE = ½mv² + ½IGω² with ω = v/r. For a thin ring IG = mr², so the rotational KE equals the translational KE.
Translational KE = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J; rotational KE = ½ × (2r²) × (3/r)² = 9 J.
Total KE = 9 + 9 = 18 J.
Exam tip: Writing only ½mv² (9 J) forgets the spin. The fraction of KE that is rotational: ring 1/2, disc 1/3, solid sphere 2/7.

questions.text: A steel rod 50 mm in diameter and 200 mm long carries an axial tensile load of 100 kN. With E = 200 GPa and Poisson's ratio 0.3, the increase in the volume of the rod is about
solution: Concept: Under a uniaxial stress the lateral strains are −νε each, so the volumetric strain is εv = ε(1 − 2ν).
V = π × 25² × 200 = 3.93 × 105 mm³, so ΔV = εvV = 40 mm³ (D). Neatly, ΔV = PL(1 − 2ν)/E, independent of the diameter.
Exam tip: ΔV = εV (100 mm³) ignores the lateral contraction; (1 + 2ν) instead of (1 − 2ν) gives 160 mm³.

questions.text: A solid circular shaft is replaced by a hollow shaft of the same material and the same outer diameter D, whose inner diameter is D/2. At the same maximum shear stress, the torque the hollow shaft can carry, as a percentage of that of the solid shaft, is
solution: Concept: T = τZp, with Zp = πD³(1 − k⁴)/16 for a hollow shaft of diameter ratio k = d/D. The material near the centre carries little stress, so removing it costs little strength.
The hollow shaft carries 93.75 % (B) of the torque, with only 1 − k² = 75 % of the material (weight).
Exam tip: 75 % (the area ratio) and 50 % (the diameter ratio) are the traps: strength goes with the polar section modulus, which depends on k⁴, not on the area.

questions.text: The cam mechanism shown has a cam (link 2) pinned to the frame (link 1), a roller (link 4) pinned to a follower (link 3) that slides in a frame guide, and rolling (higher-pair) contact between the cam and the roller. Applying Grübler's equation gives F = 2, but the mechanism has only one useful degree of freedom, because
opts: the higher pair removes two degrees of freedom
the free spin of the roller about its own pin is a redundant degree of freedom that does not affect the output motion
the follower guide is a higher pair
Grübler's equation is not valid for mechanisms with sliders
questions.ans: (B) the free spin of the roller about its own pin is a redundant degree of freedom that does not affect the output motion
solution: Concept: Grübler: F = 3(n − 1) − 2j − h. A redundant degree of freedom is a motion of a link that does not change the input–output relation.
n = 4, lower pairs j = 3 (cam pin, roller pin, follower slider), h = 1: F = 9 − 6 − 1 = 2.
The roller can spin on its pin without moving the follower, so the effective DOF = 2 − 1 = 1: option (B).

Exam tip: Grübler counts the cam–roller contact as a higher pair (rolling with slipping, h = 1). If it is taken as pure rolling without slip, it becomes a lower pair (j = 4, h = 0) and Grübler gives F = 1 directly, with no redundant freedom.

questions.text: A machine on spring mounts has a static deflection of 4 mm. Taking g = 9.81 m/s², the natural frequency of its vertical vibration (in Hz) is ______ (round off to 2 decimal places)
solution: Concept: ωn = √(k/m) = √(g/δst), since kδst = mg. fn = ωn/2π.
fn = 49.52/(2π) = 7.88 Hz (shortcut fn ≈ 15.76/√δ with δ in mm).
Exam tip: Reporting 49.5 as 'Hz' or putting δ in mm into √(g/δ) are the two common slips; always check whether rad/s or Hz is asked.

questions.text: Oil of kinematic viscosity 0.75 stoke (7.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup> m²/s) flows at a mean velocity of 1.5 m/s through a pipe of 50 mm diameter and 50 m length. Taking g = 9.81 m/s², the head lost in friction (in m) is ______ (round off to 2 decimal places)
solution: Concept: Darcy–Weisbach hf = fLV²/(2gD); for laminar flow the Darcy friction factor is f = 64/Re (the Fanning factor is 16/Re, one-quarter of it).
hf = 0.064 × (50/0.05) × 1.5²/(2 × 9.81) = 7.34 m (Hagen–Poiseuille 32μVL/(ρgD²) gives the same).
Exam tip: Using 16/Re in the Darcy formula gives 1.83 m. If the formula is written with 4f (hf = 4fLV²/2gD), then f is the Fanning factor.

questions.text: Air flows over a flat plate in laminar flow (local Nu<sub>x</sub> = 0.332 Re<sub>x</sub><sup>1/2</sup> Pr<sup>1/3</sup>). The local heat transfer coefficient at the trailing edge, x = L, is 12 W/m²·K. The average heat transfer coefficient over the whole plate (in W/m²·K) is ______
solution: Concept: In laminar flow hx ∝ x−1/2, so the average over 0 to L is havg = (1/L)∫hx dx = 2hL (Nuavg = 0.664 ReL1/2 Pr1/3).
h<sub>avg</sub> = 2 × 12.
havg = 24 W/m²·K.
Exam tip: Taking the trailing-edge value as the average underestimates the heat transfer by half. In turbulent flow (hx ∝ x−0.2) the factor is 1.25.

questions.text: A reversible heat pump delivers heat to a room at 47 °C while taking heat from the outside air at 7 °C. Its coefficient of performance is
solution: Concept: For reversible machines, COPHP = TH/(TH − TL) and COPR = TL/(TH − TL), with absolute temperatures; COPHP = COPR + 1.
T<sub>H</sub> = 320 K, T<sub>L</sub> = 280 K, T<sub>H</sub> − T<sub>L</sub> = 40 K.
Exam tip: 7.0 is the refrigerator COP; 47/40 = 1.18 uses degrees Celsius. Temperatures in COP and Carnot efficiency must be in kelvin.

questions.text: In resistance spot welding, the welding current is increased by 20 % while the resistance and the weld time remain the same. The heat generated at the joint increases by about
solution: Concept: Joule heating: H = I²Rt, so the heat varies as the square of the current.
The heat rises by 44 % (D).
Exam tip: Taking heat ∝ I gives 20 %; 2 × 20 % = 40 % is the small-change approximation that misses the 4 % square term. Current is the most powerful control in resistance welding.

questions.text: The annual demand for a part is 12 500 units. The cost of placing an order is ₹160, the unit price is ₹100 and the annual holding cost is 16 % of the unit price. The economic order quantity (in units) is ______
solution: Concept: EOQ = √(2DCo/Ch), where Ch is the holding cost per unit per year in rupees.
C<sub>h</sub> = 0.16 × 100 = ₹16 per unit per year.
Exam tip: Putting Ch = 0.16 into the formula gives 5000 units, ten times too large; always convert the holding rate into ₹ per unit per year first.
